tldr: Researchers proposed "SimEX," a framework where LLM-based coding agents acquire challenging physical robot manipulation skills from scratch without demonstrations by combining autonomous trial-and-error in simulation with only about 10 minutes of physical robot trials.
hero_caption: Overall concept of SimEX. In Stage 1, the agent trains a robust toolbox by creating and solving tasks inside a roughly correct simulation. In Stage 2, it reflects the causes of failures from a few physical trials back into the simulator, pre-screens multiple repair candidates, and applies the best one to the physical robot.
overview:
Coding agents powered by large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable results in digital domains such as software engineering and mathematical discovery. However, bringing these successes to physical robot control hits a major wall. One-shot direct code generation approaches (such as Code as Policies) often fail because LLMs are forced to guess physical parameters like calibration errors and contact dynamics. On the other hand, physical autoresearch that iteratively tests on real hardware incurs enormous costs, including hardware wear, collision risks, and the burden of constant human safety monitoring.

To solve this, the authors had a key insight: why not use simulation as a laboratory (sandbox) for the coding agent? Simulators can be manipulated freely through code, allowing agents to test rough physical laws and geometric constraints safely and quickly. The proposed method, "SimEX," operates in two stages. First, in Stage 1, without relying on human-defined reward functions or ground-truth data, the agent autonomously generates new tasks and environmental variations within the simulator to discover weaknesses in its own "toolbox" and continuously refine it. In the subsequent Stage 2, with only a few physical robot runs, the agent aligns discrepancies in the simulator based on real-world outcomes, screens multiple code repair candidates inside the simulator, and deploys only the best-performing fix to the real robot.

Experiments evaluated SimEX on three challenging tasks using a bimanual robot: folding a towel, placing a flat plate into a tote, and scanning and sorting barcodes. Despite requiring less than 10 minutes of physical robot interaction per task (5 adaptation trials), SimEX achieved 26 successes out of 30 real-world evaluation trials without any human demonstrations. This dramatically outperformed the strongest existing baseline, which succeeded only 3 times, demonstrating that an agent can gain the knowledge needed to act in the physical world using a "roughly correct simulator" without building a perfect digital twin.
contributions: Proposed "SimEX," an autoresearch framework where coding agents use simulation as a safe laboratory to efficiently acquire physical robot control capabilities.

Established an open-ended simulation autoresearch method (Stage 1) where the agent generates weakness-probing tasks and executable success predicates to expand its toolbox without requiring human-defined task distributions or evaluation metrics.

Constructed a sample-efficient adaptation method (Stage 2) that formulates multiple improvement hypotheses from failures in a few physical trials, aligns and screens them in simulation, and applies the best fix to the physical robot.

Demonstrated high success rates on three real-world tasks—contact-rich grasping, deformable cloth manipulation, and long-horizon alignment/sorting—without demonstrations and with only 10 minutes of physical interaction.

sections.heading: How Can We Safely Unleash Coding Agents into the Physical World?
sections.summary: LLM coding agents are powerful in digital spaces, but controlling physical robots poses severe challenges around physical accuracy, trial costs, and safety. SimEX solves this by positioning simulation as an agent's "laboratory" bridge, combining open-ended virtual experimentation with minimal physical trials.
sections.details:
LLM-powered coding agents have seen dramatic success in software development, such as repository-level bug fixing and automating scientific experiments. However, extending this capability to physical robot control encounters two major roadblocks.

The first is the direct generation approach, exemplified by "Code as Policies (CaP)," which synthesizes control code directly from natural language prompts. While it requires no physical trial and error, it relies heavily on sophisticated, human-engineered perception and motion planning primitives. Without such primitives, the LLM has to blindly guess physical parameters not present in the prompt or training data, such as tiny camera calibration offsets or exact contact grasping positions, leading to frequent failures on demanding real-world tasks.

The second is the "physical autoresearch" approach, which mirrors software self-improvement by running trial-and-error loops directly on physical robots. While learning directly from real-world feedback is beneficial, it introduces massive experimental costs and safety concerns, including robot operating time, risks of collision-induced damage, and the burden of building automated environment reset mechanisms.

To overcome these hurdles, the authors proposed a core idea: make the simulator a bridge between the coding agent and the physical world. Because simulators can be written and controlled in code, they integrate seamlessly with LLMs, enabling thousands of safe trials over physical laws and geometric constraints. Of course, simulators cannot perfectly replicate reality. However, SimEX overcomes this imperfection by designing a two-stage pipeline: the agent builds a base of general procedures and operational limit knowledge inside a "roughly correct simulator," and then bridges the real-world gap using only a small handful of physical robot experiences.

captions.F1: Overall workflow of SimEX. In Stage 1 (top), general skills are developed through an open-ended loop inside the simulation. In Stage 2 (middle), every physical robot run triggers extensive simulator-side testing of multiple repair candidates for efficient adaptation. The bottom row shows snapshots of successful physical robot executions using the optimized toolbox.

sections.heading: Self-Play in Simulation and Fast Screening for Physical Robots
sections.summary: SimEX starts by constructing a workspace simulation. It then optimizes a reusable "toolbox" across two stages: Stage 1 autonomously discovers and addresses weaknesses in simulation, and Stage 2 screens repair candidates in the simulator using feedback from physical trials.
sections.details:
Rather than optimizing one-off task-specific scripts, SimEX optimizes a reusable "toolbox." This toolbox consists of a pair: Python code implementing perception and control primitives (toolbox.py), and documentation detailing when to use these functions, their measured limits, and known failure modes (skill.md).

### 2.1 Problem Formulation
When faced with a new task, the LLM generates an executable program following the CaP paradigm by referencing the current toolbox.py and skill.md. The toolbox relies strictly on raw RGB-D images and low-level robot APIs (such as inverse kinematics and Cartesian/joint position commands), without privileged environment states or human-crafted high-level skills. The entire optimization operates as an autonomous loop where the agent rewrites code according to prompt instructions, testing and evaluating iteratively through an execution harness.

### 2.2 Preparation: Simulation Environment Construction
First, a rough simulation environment (sandbox) is built from workspace photos of the physical setup. It does not need to be a photorealistic, perfect digital twin; the coding agent selects suitable assets from a 3D mesh library to roughly replicate the geometric layout. Initial perception modules and API documentation are initialized at the same time.

### 2.3 Stage 1: Open-Ended Capability Discovery in Simulation
Simply optimizing for a target task in the newly created simulator risks overfitting to simulation-specific physics. Thus, in Stage 1, the agent autonomously drives an "explore-focus-optimize" cycle:
- Step 1 (Capability Exploration): The agent generates diverse environmental variations—altering object mass, friction, initial poses, and goal conditions—along with executable predicate code to evaluate success. This stress-tests its current toolbox to expose weaknesses.
- Step 2 (Subgoal Focusing): It selects one systematic weakness from the exposed failures and fixes a training task set dedicated to improving it.
- Step 3 (Subgoal-Driven Autoresearch): The agent iteratively rewrites toolbox.py and skill.md through simulated experimentation, hill-climbing its performance. To prevent catastrophic forgetting, it uses a "capability bank replay" mechanism that samples and co-evaluates previously solved tasks. In addition, it employs "population-based optimization" running four independent optimization processes; these share experiment notes but are prohibited from copying code directly, preserving exploratory diversity.

### 2.4 Stage 2: Simulation-Assisted Few-Trial Physical Adaptation
The toolbox refined in Stage 1 is deployed to the physical robot, but it may fail due to the Sim-to-Real gap. Stage 2 bridges this gap in only about 5 physical trials. The defining feature is that upon a physical failure, rather than blindly testing another fix on hardware, the agent transforms one painful failure into dozens of simulator-side experiments:
- It records execution logs (videos, images, execution traces) from the physical run and replays the identical control code inside the simulator.
- If the simulator's behavior diverges from reality, the agent first adjusts simulator parameters or definitions to match the replayed behavior (simulator alignment).
- Next, it formulates multiple distinct hypotheses explaining the failure and writes candidate repair implementations for each hypothesis.
- These candidates undergo parallel screening in the simulator (reproduction and generalization tests). The agent examines the resulting logs and selects only the single most promising fix to deploy in the next physical trial.

captions.F2: Detailed pipeline of SimEX. In Preparation, the environment is roughly reconstructed from images. In Stage 1 (blue), parallel explore-focus-optimize cycles expand the toolbox. In Stage 2 (orange), a single physical trial branches into simulator alignment and multi-candidate screening.

sections.heading: Unlocking Complex Tasks with Only 10 Minutes of Physical Interaction
sections.summary: SimEX was evaluated across three task families: plate manipulation, towel folding, and barcode scanning. In both rigorous Sim-to-Sim comparisons and physical robot experiments, SimEX substantially outperformed baselines, achieving 26 successes out of 30 physical trials.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations used a bimanual YAM robot across three challenging task families (21 evaluation tasks in total):
- Plate to tote: Flat plates resting on a table cannot be grasped from directly above; the agent must discover geometric grasping strategies that pinch the rim from the side.
- Towel folding: A deformable manipulation task highly sensitive to friction, pinch points, and dragging trajectories.
- Barcode scanning: A long-horizon task requiring the robot to pick up an item, orient its barcode face toward a stationary scanner, read it, and deposit it into another container.
All adaptation methods were given a physical adaptation budget of 5 trials (roughly 10 minutes). Toolboxes were frozen after optimization for evaluation.

### 3.2 Controlled Sim-to-Sim Evaluation
To collect fair and extensive statistics, tests were conducted across entirely different physics engines (the sandbox used MuJoCo/FLASH, while the evaluation environment used Isaac Sim/MJWarp Flex). Across all 21 tasks, SimEX matched or exceeded all baselines (such as direct CaP generation, physical-only adaptation with ENPIRE, and zero-shot transfer with DrEureka). In the longest-horizon barcode scanning task, where the best baseline achieved at most 18% success, SimEX reached an average success rate of 85%. Incorporating simulator-based repair screening in Stage 2 more than doubled the performance gain achieved per deployment.

### 3.3 Physical Robot Evaluation
One representative task from each family was deployed on the physical YAM robot (10 trials each, 30 trials total). The results were striking: SimEX succeeded in 26 out of 30 trials (Plate: 9/10, Towel: 9/10, Barcode: 8/10). In contrast, the strongest baseline achieved only 3 total successes, with all baselines failing completely on the two-object barcode scanning task. Qualitatively, the robot naturally learned adaptive behaviors, such as switching which gripper grasped the plate depending on its distance to the tote, and smoothing out wrinkles after folding the towel.

### 3.4 Ablations and Agent Comparisons
Ablation experiments revealed that population diversity and capability bank replay in Stage 1 are critical for maintaining performance. Furthermore, substituting Fable 5.1 with other LLMs (Opus 5, GPT-5.5, and GPT-6 Astra) maintained SimEX's dominance, consistently outperforming baselines by over 50 percentage points. As base model reasoning capability improved (from 67% with GPT-5.5 to 82% with GPT-6 Astra), overall system performance increased accordingly.

captions.F6: Success rate comparison on the barcode scanning task across different coding agents (Fable 5.1, Opus 5, GPT-5.5, and GPT-6 Astra). Regardless of the underlying agent, SimEX (bottom bar) significantly outpaces other methods, and stronger agent reasoning correlates with higher overall system performance.

sections.heading: Prior Work vs. SimEX: A Laboratory for Knowledge, Not Just a Policy Learner
sections.summary: Compared to prior work in LLM robot control, autoresearch, and Sim-to-Real transfer, SimEX fundamentally differs by treating simulation not as a training data generator for a single policy, but as an interactive laboratory where an agent inspects and refines a code-based perception and control toolbox.
sections.details:
SimEX sits at the intersection of four primary research areas:

- LLM-Based Robot Control: While generating robot plans or code directly from language instructions (such as Code as Policies) is widely studied, these methods assume pre-existing, human-crafted high-level APIs and perception modules. SimEX differs by enabling the agent to autonomously build and calibrate these foundational manipulation primitives through experimentation.
- Agentic Optimization (AutoResearch): Autonomous research loops that iteratively rewrite code to improve performance have shown strong results in software engineering and theorem proving. Prior attempts to apply this to robotics (like ENPIRE) relied on physical trials, creating prohibitive burdens around reset mechanisms and safety. SimEX drastically slashes these costs by using simulation as its primary laboratory.
- Generative Simulation and Environment Design: Using foundation models to generate simulation environments and tasks is increasingly popular, but mostly focused on generating training data for reinforcement learning policies. SimEX uses environment generation as a tool to stress-test and reveal weaknesses in the agent's symbolic code toolbox.
- Sim-to-Real Transfer: Traditional Sim-to-Real focuses on transferring a single fixed policy to reality via domain randomization or high-fidelity simulation. In contrast, SimEX transfers code and documentation describing measured physical limits and general procedures rather than neural network weights. Consequently, as long as the physics are qualitatively sound, a rough simulator is sufficient to extract knowledge that adapts well to the real world.

sections.heading: Simulation Is a Potent Weapon—Even When It's Only "Roughly Correct"
sections.summary: SimEX dramatically streamlines physical robot control for coding agents through open-ended exploration in a rough simulator and a simulator-verified adaptation loop for real-world failures. It proves that a simulator can serve as an effective laboratory without being a perfect digital twin.
sections.details:
This paper introduced SimEX, an autoresearch framework that uses simulation as a bridge between coding agents and physical robots. The two-stage design—fostering a robust toolbox through open-ended exploration unconstrained by fixed metrics in Stage 1, followed by feeding real-world failures into the simulator to screen repair candidates in Stage 2—proved exceptionally effective.

The key takeaway for robotics is that a simulator does not need to millimeter-perfectly mimic reality to be valuable for acquiring physical intelligence. What the agent carries over from simulation is not an overfitted low-level control policy, but procedural knowledge and physical boundary awareness grounded in qualitative physical behavior.

Current limitations include evaluating only on a single bimanual robot platform (YAM) and relying on a human operator to reset the workspace between Stage 2 physical trials. Future work expanding to different robot morphologies and automating the reset behaviors will pave the way toward fully autonomous physical coding agents.

sections.heading: Implementation Details, Task Specs, and Comparison with Online Inference
sections.summary: The appendix details prompt structures, operational costs, initial state setups across the 21 tasks, and an important comparison between programmatic generation and online agent control.
sections.details:
### Implementation and Prompts
All executed task programs are generated via a single text call (following Code as Policies) combining skill.md, toolbox.py, and the task prompt. Task-level inference takes only about 30 seconds. While toolbox optimization requires reasoning tokens, execution is extremely lightweight once the toolbox is established.

### Task Family Specifications
- Plate to tote: Lifting a flat plate by at least 5 cm and placing it in a container. Includes 7 variations with different plate positions and tilted totes.
- Towel folding: Manipulating towels of 56×36 cm or 34×34 cm to match target shapes, such as translation, area reduction, single fold, and double fold. Simply bunching the cloth into a ball is marked as a failure.
- Barcode scanning: Grasping bottles or rectangular blocks, exposing barcodes occluded against walls or bases to a scanner, and placing them in separate bins. Scenarios with multiple objects require reasoning over grasping order.

### Comparison with Online Agent Control
The authors compared SimEX's programmatic generation against an "Online Agent Control" baseline that sequentially predicts low-level actions upon receiving each image. The online approach required approximately 30 LLM calls per trial, spending over 40 minutes just waiting for model responses (more than 50 times the robot's physical movement time) and failing to complete any task within the time limit. This underscores the practical superiority of SimEX's design, which moves LLM reasoning outside the real-time execution loop to synthesize executable programs in advance.

captions.F7: Layout of the three experimental workspaces on the physical robot: (a) Plate to tote, (b) Towel folding, and (c) Barcode scanning and sorting. All tasks share the same bimanual YAM robot and workspace booth, while presenting distinct physical and geometric challenges.

takeaways: A simulator does not need to be a high-fidelity digital twin; its true value is acting as a "roughly correct laboratory" where an agent tests qualitative physical boundaries and algorithms.

When a physical trial fails, reflecting physical execution logs into the simulator to screen multiple candidate repairs dramatically increases sample efficiency over immediate physical trial-and-error.
Developing a reusable "toolbox" combining perception/control primitives and a manual (skill.md)—rather than directly optimizing task-specific scripts—vastly improves generality and reusability.

Embedding LLMs directly into real-time control loops (online policies) collapses under latency; synthesizing and verifying executable Python programs offline prior to execution is far more practical for real-world robotics.
limitations: In Stage 2 physical adaptation, workspace resetting (object re-initialization) between trials was handled by a human operator, leaving full automation unachieved.
Evaluations were restricted to a single bimanual robot platform (YAM) and booth environment; generalizability to mobile robots or different manipulators requires further validation.
Initializing the Stage 1 sandbox still requires prompt setup and a pre-assembled library of rough 3D meshes.
